# Seventy-Two Hours

## I.

The crime-scene tape hung from the left basket stanchion like a stripped pennant. Someone from the department had wound it twice around the pole and then, apparently losing interest or running out of tape, had tied it off in a knot that drooped toward the free-throw line. No one had removed it. In four days no one from the university had entered the gymnasium at all, and the tape had settled into the stillness of the place and become part of it, the way a scar becomes part of a face.

Deshawn Mallory wheeled through the double doors at 9:07 on a Tuesday morning and stopped her chair at center court. She set her phone face-down on her thigh. She had been captain for three seasons, point guard for four, and she had called meetings in this gym perhaps forty times—before road trips, after losses, once when the administration tried to cut their travel funding. She had never called one like this.

They came in ones and twos. The gym had no air conditioning in the off-season, and the late-June heat had thickened the air until it tasted of varnish and old rubber. The floor was clean. The custodial staff, at least, had done their work. There was no mark where Marcus Flood had lain, no stain, no residue. Only the tape on the stanchion. Only the particular quality of silence in a room where something has been taken that cannot be replaced.

---

Carmen Ojeda arrived first, as she always did. She was the center—six foot one in her chair, with hands that could palm a basketball the way most people palm an orange, and eyes that moved over mouths and faces with the fluency of someone reading a novel in her first language. Carmen had been deaf since birth. Her hearing aids gave her enough to track a referee's whistle and the buzzer, but conversation was something she took from lips, from the architecture of jaw and tongue, and she was better at it than anyone Deshawn had ever met. She could read a coach's halftime adjustments from across the court. She could catch a stranger's phone call from thirty feet away if the angle was right.

She had read one such call eleven days ago. Marcus Flood, standing outside the athletics building, phone pressed to his ear, speaking to someone whose identity Carmen did not know. She had caught fragments—not all of it, not yet, she told herself—and the fragments had kept her awake for six nights running. She parked her chair to Deshawn's left and folded her hands in her lap. In her mind the fragment played on a loop, the shape of Marcus's lips forming the words she had not yet shared in full: *I'm going to the board with all of it, the classification, the payments, everything.* Carmen knew what "the payments" meant. She had found, in the recycling bin outside Coach Davenport's office, a bank statement that did not belong there, and the amounts listed corresponded to nothing legitimate and to everything she suspected. Coach Andrea Davenport was being blackmailed, or was blackmailing someone, or both—the direction of the money was not something Carmen had been able to determine, and she had not tried very hard, because trying hard would have meant asking questions she could not unask.

She knew about the payments. She knew about the phone call. She did not know what "the classification" meant, and so she waited, and said nothing, and watched Deshawn's mouth.

---

Tanya Osei wheeled in next, the shooting guard, all precision and economy even in the way she crossed the threshold—one clean push, a coast, a stop. Tanya's mother was Dr. Abena Osei, chief of emergency medicine at St. Clare's, and Tanya had grown up in hospitals the way other children grew up in parks. She understood triage. She understood records. She understood, with a specificity that she kept carefully invisible, how to access the patient management system at St. Clare's using her mother's login, which her mother changed quarterly and which Tanya had been quietly noting for two years—not out of malice, not even out of curiosity, but out of the same compulsion that made her shoot two hundred free throws a day: the need to know where things were, to have the numbers, to be sure.

She had used that access two nights ago. She had searched for Marcus Flood's name and found him. He had visited the ER nine days before his death, complaining of a fall from his adapted bicycle. The injuries—bruising along the left ribcage, a hairline fracture of the fourth metacarpal—were not consistent with a bicycle fall. They were consistent with being struck. The attending physician's name was entered in the system with bureaucratic indifference: Dr. Nathan Davenport. The coach's husband.

Tanya had printed nothing. She had taken a photograph of the screen with her phone, and the photograph sat in a locked folder, and the folder sat in her chest like a stone.

---

Then came Jessie Woo and Araceli Fuentes, the forwards, orbiting each other as they always did—Jessie talking, Araceli listening, their chairs moving in the practiced tandem of players who had run the pick-and-roll together so many times that their bodies thought in pairs. Jessie knew only what the news knew: Marcus Flood, equipment manager, found dead in the gymnasium, blunt-force trauma, and the arrest two days later of Dennis Okafor, the former coach who had been fired three years ago for what the university called "philosophical differences" and what everyone on the team called rage. Araceli knew the same. They were frightened and grieving in the uncomplicated way of people who have nothing to hide, and the omniscient eye that moves through this story pauses on them only to note the particular mercy of their ignorance. They sat together. Jessie cracked her knuckles. Araceli stared at the tape on the stanchion.

---

Last through the doors, four minutes late and apologizing to no one, was Riley Chen.

Riley was the bench player. She had been the bench player for three years. She entered games in the fourth quarter of blowouts, wins and losses alike, when the outcome was determined and the minutes were ceremonial. She averaged 1.3 points per game, 0.7 assists, and a plus-minus so close to zero that it constituted a kind of statistical invisibility. She was also the team's administrative volunteer—she filed the travel paperwork, organized the equipment inventory, laminated the practice schedules, and processed the disability classification forms that the International Paralympic Committee required for competition. She did this because someone had to and because no one else wanted to, and because Riley had learned long ago that the person who handles the paperwork sees everything and is seen by no one.

Seven months earlier, she had processed Deshawn Mallory's reclassification documents. The documents stated that Deshawn's spinal cord injury was at the T6 level, which placed her in the 2.0 functional classification—the category assigned to players with significant limitation in trunk movement and lower-limb function. Riley had watched Deshawn practice. She had seen the micro-adjustments, the compensatory movements, the particular way Deshawn's torso rotated when she drove to the basket. Riley's own classification was 1.0. She knew what a 2.0 body looked like, and Deshawn's body did not look like that. Deshawn's injury was higher than T6 or her functional capacity was greater—either way, the paperwork was wrong, and the wrongness was not accidental. A properly classified Deshawn would have pushed the team's total point value over the on-court maximum. A properly classified Deshawn could not play.

Riley had filed the paperwork. She had said nothing. She had told herself that Deshawn deserved to play—that the classification system was an imperfect instrument measuring an irreducible reality, that the difference between a 2.0 and a 2.5 was a line drawn in sand, that the team needed its point guard. She had told herself these things and they were partly true and partly the sound a person makes when she is choosing loyalty over honesty and needs the choosing to feel like reason.

She wheeled into the circle. She parked between Araceli and Carmen, slightly behind both, and she watched.

---

Six chairs on the gymnasium floor. The tape on the stanchion moved in a draft from somewhere. Deshawn looked at each of them and felt the particular weight of being the one who speaks first.

"You all know why we're here," she said. "And you know why it can't be campus police doing this."

"Because they already think they've got their man," Jessie said.

"Because Okafor confessed," Deshawn said. She picked up her phone, unlocked it, and read aloud.

The confession had been transcribed in the police report, which Deshawn had obtained through a method she did not explain and no one questioned. Dennis Okafor's words filled the gym like an incantation. He had dictated it himself, the report noted, refusing the detective's offer to simply answer questions. He wanted it in his own language. He got it.

"'I went to the gymnasium at approximately eleven-fifteen p.m.,'" Deshawn read. "'I knew he would be there because he was always there, tending to equipment that was beneath him, organizing a program that had been taken from me and given to someone who did not understand what I had built. I want to be clear: I did not act in a moment of passion. I had carried this intention for some time. It had become a companion. Marcus Flood was a functionary who mistook proximity to greatness for participation in it, and when he began to make threats—threats I will not dignify by repeating—I understood that the removal of such a person was not violence but correction. I struck him with the hand weight from the training rack, third shelf, twenty-pound plate. I struck him once. He fell. I did not check for a pulse because I did not need to. I left through the loading dock. I drove home. I slept well.'"

Silence. The tape on the stanchion swayed.

"It sounds wrong," Carmen said, and because speech was not her native medium, the words carried the particular authority of something she had chosen to say aloud rather than sign.

"It sounds rehearsed," Tanya said.

"It sounds *literary,*" said Jessie.

"It sounds like a man who wanted to have done it," Araceli said, surprising everyone, including herself.

Deshawn set her phone down. "It does," she said. "It sounds exactly like that."

What Deshawn did not say—what the omniscient narration must now say for her, with something approaching tenderness—was that she had read the confession fourteen times and fixed on the phrase *when he began to make threats* with the focus of a woman staring at her own X-ray. She knew what threats Marcus had been making. She knew because Marcus had told her, three weeks ago, in this gymnasium, standing near the stanchion where the tape now hung. He had been kind about it. He had said, *Deshawn, I like you, and I don't want to do this, but I found the classification paperwork, and it's wrong, and you know it's wrong.* He had given her two weeks. The two weeks had expired four days before his death, and Deshawn had done nothing, because Deshawn had not known what to do, and then Marcus was dead, and the two weeks became meaningless, and Okafor confessed, and for forty-eight hours Deshawn had allowed herself to feel the dizzying reprieve of a crisis someone else had resolved—until she read the confession and heard in its cadences not the voice of a killer but the voice of a man performing a killing he had not done.

The confession was wrong. She was almost sure it was wrong. And she needed it to be wrong, not because she wanted justice—though she did, she insisted to herself that she did—but because if Okafor was guilty, then Marcus's death and Deshawn's secret were unrelated, and she could go on playing, and the team could go on existing, and the championship in seventy-two hours could go on meaning what it was supposed to mean. But if Okafor was innocent, then someone else had killed Marcus, and the reason might be tangled in the very thing Marcus had threatened to expose, and the act of investigating was also the act of approaching her own unmaking.

She chose to investigate. The choice was genuinely brave and slightly desperate in equal measure, and the omniscient voice notes both without choosing between them.

"Here's what I'm thinking," Deshawn said. "Carmen—you told me last week that you saw Marcus on a phone call the day before he died. That you read some of it."

Carmen nodded.

"I need you to get me the rest. Everything you caught. Every word."

Carmen's hands tightened in her lap. She had shared only a fragment with Deshawn—the phrase *going to the board*—and had withheld the rest because the rest included words she did not yet understand and words she understood too well. She nodded again.

"Tanya. Your mom works at St. Clare's. Marcus went to the ER two weeks ago—it's in the campus police report, just a line, 'victim recently treated for minor injuries.' I need to know what those injuries were. I need to know who treated him."

Tanya said, "I'll see what I can find." She said it evenly. She did not mention that she had already found it.

"Jessie, Araceli—I need you to talk to the other staff. The custodians, the front-desk people, anyone who might have seen something that night. You're the most likable people on this team. Use it."

Jessie grinned. Araceli managed a quarter-smile.

"Riley," Deshawn said, and her gaze moved to the bench player with the reflexive half-attention of someone addressing a supporting character. "You've got access to the equipment room, the office, the files. See if Marcus left anything—notes, emails, anything he was working on."

"Okay," Riley said.

The meeting was over. They broke the circle. Wheels turned on the glossy wood. The gymnasium emptied in ones and twos, the same way it had filled, and when the last chair cleared the double doors, the tape on the stanchion was still there, hanging at the angle of something no one had decided to address, not torn down, not straightened, just present—marking the place where a thing had happened that was not yet understood, in a room that would have to hold what came next.

---

## II.

Thirty-six hours before the championship, at four in the afternoon, the heat in the borrowed classroom where they met was cut by a single window unit that rattled at intervals and accomplished nothing. They had migrated here from the gymnasium two days into the investigation—Jessie had said she couldn't think in the gym anymore, couldn't stop looking at the stanchion—and the classroom, unused for the summer, had become theirs by squatter's right. A portable whiteboard leaned against the wall with a timeline Deshawn had built in blue marker: dates, names, arrows. It looked like a coach's play diagram. The resemblance was not lost on anyone.

They were supposed to have a full session today—all six—but Jessie and Araceli had texted to say they were still tracking down Ricardo, the night custodian, who had called in sick three shifts running and was not answering his phone. That investigation—the external one, the safe one, the one that pointed away from the center of the circle—was going nowhere slowly, and Jessie's last message had carried the tone of someone losing faith in her assignment: *he's probably just scared. everyone's scared.*

So there were four of them: Deshawn, Carmen, Tanya, and Riley.

Tanya spoke first. She had decided in the night—after two hours of staring at her ceiling and running the calculations one more time—that withholding the hospital records any longer was a betrayal of something she wasn't willing to betray. She spoke in the clipped, clinical language she had inherited from her mother, as if the facts would be less dangerous delivered without inflection.

"Marcus went to the ER on June ninth. He told them he fell off his bike. The injuries don't match that story. He had bruising on his left ribs—patterned, like a grip or repeated impact—and a fracture in his right hand, fourth metacarpal, the kind you get from hitting something or someone. Or the kind you get from trying to stop something from hitting you."

She paused.
